content: Cephalanthus occidentalis, commonly known as Buttonbush, Button-willow, or Honey-bells, is a plant species native to the eastern and southern regions of North America. It is a deciduous shrub or small tree that typically grows to a height of 2 to 10 meters, although in rare cases, it can reach up to 15 meters. The leaves of Cephalanthus occidentalis are arranged either in opposite pairs or in whorls of three. They are elliptic to ovate in shape, measuring between 7 and 20 centimeters in length and 3 to 7 centimeters in width. The leaf margins are smooth (entire), and the leaves are attached to the stem by a short petiole. The flowers of this species are organized into dense, spherical inflorescences that are 2.5 to 3.5 centimeters in diameter. These inflorescences are borne on peduncles that are 2.5 to 5 centimeters long. Each individual flower has a tubular corolla that is fused and features four lobes. The corolla is white to pale yellow in color and forms a long, slender tube that connects to the calyx. The stigma of the flower is elongated and extends approximately 4 millimeters beyond the corolla. There are two recognized varieties of Cephalanthus occidentalis, although not all taxonomic authorities consider them to be distinct: 1. Cephalanthus occidentalis var. occidentalis (synonym: var. pubescens) – This variety, commonly referred to as the Common Buttonbush, is found in eastern North America, ranging from Nova Scotia westward to Minnesota and southward to Florida and eastern Texas. 2. Cephalanthus occidentalis var. californicus – Known as the California Button-willow, this variety is native to southwestern North America. Its range extends from western Texas westward to California, including regions such as the Sierra Nevada foothills, the San Joaquin Valley, the Sacramento Valley, and the Inner North Coast Ranges. It is also found further south in Mexico and Central America.
